Aneurysm of the Aorta

Slide 64
  • Clinical features:
  • Symptoms and signs of an aneurysm arise from:
  • Compression of surrounding structures.
  • Erosion of surrounding bone.
  • Rupture or leakage of blood.
  • Its manifestations depend on the site of the aneurysm.

Aneurysm of the Ascending Aorta:

Slide 65
  • This is called aneurysm of the signs as it produces many signs and few symptoms:
  • The aneurysm produces dullness and palpable pulsations in second right intercostal space.
  • Compression and obstruction of the superior vena cava result in dilated non-pulsating neck veins and congestion of the face, arms and chest.
  • Compression of the right bronchus and lung causes collapse.
  • Erosion of the sternum may produce a pulsating mass.
  • Cardiac signs:
  • Aortic regurge.
  • L.V. enlargement from a.R.

Aneurysm of the Aortic Arch:

Slide 66
  • This is called aneurysm of symptoms:
  • Compression of the trachea results in cough, dyspnea, hoarseness of voice.
  • Compression of the esophagus results in dysphagia
  • Compression of RLN produces hoarseness of voice.
  • Pressure on the arteries leads to unequal pulses.
  • Erosion of the vertebrae causes deep-seated pain in the back.

Aortic Aneurysm

Slide 68
  • Commonly accepted criteria for surgical intervention on ascending Aortic aneurysm:
  • Sporadic: > 5.5cm
  • Connective tissue disorders: 4.5-5cm
  • Bicuspid aortic valve: 5 cm
  • Concomitant cardiac surgery: > 4.5cm
  • Growth of aneurysm > 0.5cm/year
  • Symptoms due to the aneurysm

Surgery for Cardio-thoracic Diseases

Aortic Dissection

Slide 69
  • Type A dissections
  • Involving the ascending aorta
  • Are a medical emergency and require immediate surgery.
  • Mortality rate up to 1-2% per hour.
  • Type B dissections
  • Arising in the descending aorta
  • Carry a lower mortality rate and can be managed medically, TEVAR, or surgically.
  • May cause symptoms due to vascular compromise to other areas e.g. acute limb ischemia, renal ischemia, paraplegia, mesenteric ischemia.

Surgery for Cardio-thoracic Diseases

Added explanationInvestigations & management (added): CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice (TOE if unstable). Start IV beta-blocker (target HR < 60, SBP 100–120) and analgesia. Type A → emergency surgery (replace the ascending aorta ± valve). Type B → medical control; TEVAR for complications (malperfusion, rupture, expansion, refractory pain).
Slide 70Aortic Dissection
  • DeBakey classification system
  • Type I - Originates in ascending aorta, propagates at least to the aortic arch and often beyond it distally.
  • Type II – Originates in and is confined to the ascending aorta.
  • Type III – Originates in descending aorta, rarely extends proximally but will extend distally.
  • Daily (Stanford) classification system
  • Divided into 2 groups; A and B depending on whether the ascending aorta is involved.
  • A = Type I and II DeBakey
  • B = Type III DeBakey

Clinical picture:

Slide 71
  • Pain: very sudden onset with severe tearing retrosternal pain that resembles that of myocardial infarction but radiates to the back, neck, abdomen and legs.
  • Aortic regurgitation in some cases.
  • Involvement of great vessels produces unequal pulses, neurologic signs, renal pain, paraplegia etc.
  • Left side pleural effusion
  • Involvement of RCA leads to ischemic pain or M.I.
  • The patient is usually hypertensive.

Differential Diagnosis:

Slide 72
  • Aortic dissection is most commonly confused with M.I.
  • It can be differentiated from it by:
  • The pain is of very abrupt onset and radiates to the back and abdomen.
  • Presence of unequal upper limb pulses or weak femoral pulses.
  • Presence of aortic regurgitation
  • Wide mediastinum in the chest x-ray.s
